findings.title: Strategy close() shuts down the factory-shared queue pool; the next rebalance silently drops and commits messages
findings.body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`, `terminate()` and `join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`. That pool is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and reused by every strategy from `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`. Arroyo closes the strategy and calls `create_with_partitions` again on every partition rebalance. After the first rebalance the new strategy therefore gets a pool whose workers have exited and whose queues are shut down. `queue.put` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit()` catches that with its generic `except Exception`, calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset`, and the offset becomes committable. The result is that every message after a rebalance is dropped and its offset committed, which is data loss. The pool should be created per strategy, or the strategy should not own the shared pool's lifecycle. The `OffsetTracker` is also shared across rebalances, so stale offsets and `last_committed` for revoked partitions persist.

findings.title: Any failure while enqueuing is treated as 'processed' and the offset is committed
findings.body: The broad `except Exception` in `submit()` logs the error, then registers and immediately completes the offset. That includes failures of `queue_pool.submit` (for example `queue.ShutDown`) and of `grouping_fn`. The offset becomes committable and the message is permanently skipped. Only decode failures (result is None) should be skipped this way. Infrastructure errors should be raised or retried so the message is not lost.

findings.title: Claimed backpressure does not exist; queues and offset tracker are unbounded
findings.body: The docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. The queues are `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, `submit()` never blocks, and `poll()` never raises `MessageRejected`. If one queue is slow, which is the scenario this PR targets, the consumer keeps reading from Kafka. Messages accumulate in memory without bound. `all_offsets` grows with them, and so does the per-commit `range()` scan. The consumer can run out of memory, and the offset stuck at the slow item can never advance. Use bounded queues and reject or block when full.

findings.title: Kafka commit callback is invoked from a background thread
findings.body: `commit_function` (arroyo's `commit`) is called from `_commit_loop`, a separate daemon thread, while the StreamProcessor main thread is polling and managing the consumer. Arroyo's commit callback and the Kafka consumer state are designed to be used from the processing thread. Calling them concurrently risks races and corrupted offset state. The commit is also not tied to partition ownership, so offsets can be committed for partitions already revoked during a rebalance. Commits should be issued from `poll()`/`submit()` in the main thread.

findings.title: Non-contiguous Kafka offsets stall commits forever
findings.body: Commit advancement requires every integer offset in the range to be present in `all_offsets`. Offsets that are never delivered to the strategy (transaction control markers, compacted or skipped offsets) look like a permanent gap. Commits for that partition then stall indefinitely and `all_offsets` and `outstanding` grow without bound. The gap test encodes this as intended behaviour. A tracker keyed on submitted offsets (commit up to the lowest outstanding offset minus one) would avoid it.

findings.title: Error-handling test contradicts the implementation and its own docstring
findings.body: The test docstring says errors in processing 'don't block offset commits'. The implementation completes the offset in a `finally` block even when processing fails, so offsets 100 and 101 are committed (as 102). The assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` expects no commit. It passes only because the wait loop ends before the 1-second commit loop fires, so it is timing-dependent. It verifies nothing about the intended behaviour and will fail or flake as timing changes.

findings.title: Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing
findings.body: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys cover all 3 queues. The queue index comes from `hash(str)`, which is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). There is a small but non-zero chance (about 0.1%) that a queue is missed, so the test can fail occasionally.
